name: Regulatory and eligibility constraints for this founding team (market-analysis level, not legal advice)
summary: The founding team's regulatory position is workable but path-dependent. SBIR/STTR authority lapsed on 2025-09-30 and was restored by S. 3971 (signed 2026-04-13, authorized through 2031), but the 13 CFR 121.702 test (more than 50 percent owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or permanent residents) means the Indonesian founder's equity never counts toward eligibility and the German founder's counts only once permanent residence is granted; DoD SBIR components (e.g., AFWERX) additionally restrict foreign-national work to public-domain or fundamental research. Other Transactions and CSOs (10 U.S.C. 4022, 3014) carry no statutory ownership test and are the most accessible federal path, subject to export-control and eventual FOCI/CUI constraints written into individual solicitations. Under ITAR (22 CFR 120.62) and the EAR deemed-export rule a permanent resident is a U.S. person, but under the NISP/FOCI regime (32 CFR 117) any non-citizen, including a green-card holder, is a 'foreign interest', and personnel clearances require citizenship, so any classified-dependent model is 5+ years away for both founders and would require cleared U.S.-citizen key management personnel plus FOCI mitigation. Export classification is the pivotal design decision: generic C2/COP/data-fabric software built on commercial components and not 'specially designed' for a USML article generally sits under the EAR (EAR99 or 5D002), which imposes little friction on an Indonesian or German engineer, whereas anything specially designed for fire control, EW, military sensors, Link 16 or military UAS drifts into 600-series or USML control with deemed-export licensing for the Indonesian founder. CMMC's DFARS clause took effect 2025-11-10 with Phase 1 self-assessments; DoD suspended the Phase 2 (C3PAO) transition in July 2026, which reduces near-term certification cost but not the underlying NIST SP 800-171 obligation once CUI flows. TAK (ATAK-CIV and SDK, open-sourced by the TAK Product Center) is the lowest-friction unclassified entry point, alongside public-safety COP, commercial-imagery PED, data-integration middleware, DevSecOps/edge tooling and unclassified M&S. Segment-level burden ranges from low (TAK plugins, edge/DevSecOps, M&S) to inherently controlled (EW, cross-domain solutions, targeting/fire control, SIGINT PED, space C2). Specialist counsel must review export classification (CJ/CCATS), a technology control plan, SBIR ownership computation and timing, FOCI/CFIUS exposure at fundraising, CMMC scoping, TAK license terms and immigration timelines before capital is committed.

findings.title: SBIR/STTR lapsed 2025-09-30 and was reauthorized 2026-04-13 through 2031
findings.detail: Statutory authority for SBIR/STTR lapsed on 2025-09-30; agencies stopped issuing new solicitations and awards (e.g., NIH Notice NOT-OD-26-006 of 2025-11-17 closed open opportunities). The Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act (S. 3971) passed the Senate 2026-03-03 and the House 2026-03-17 and was signed 2026-04-13, extending authorization to 2031-09-30.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: SBIR/STTR authority lapsed on September 30, 2025 and was restored by S. 3971, signed into law April 13, 2026, extending authorization through September 30, 2031.
findings.source_title: SBIR/STTR Programs Reauthorized After Six-Month Lapse (Crowell & Moring); Congress Reauthorizes SBIR/STTR (IEDC)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: SBIR is again available but the six-month gap compressed FY26 cycles; the German founder's permanent-residence timing determines when the company can even self-certify eligibility.

findings.title: The 2026 reauthorization reportedly rewrote award and eligibility rules; specifics not verified this session
findings.detail: Law-firm commentary (Fox Rothschild: 'Rewriting the Rules'; Covington's Inside Government Contracts, March 2026; CSIS analysis) indicates S. 3971 changed program rules beyond a simple extension. The enacted text could not be read this session (egress blocked). Whether the ownership test, foreign-ties bars, award caps or repeat-awardee limits changed must be confirmed against the statute.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase of titles: Congress revives SBIR/STTR programs, rewriting the rules for small business innovation funding.
findings.source_title: Congress Revives SBIR/STTR Programs, Rewriting the Rules (Fox Rothschild); Is Congress Finally Reauthorizing SBIR/STTR and What's Changing (Inside Government Contracts)
findings.label: HYPOTHESIS
findings.startup_relevance: Any plan built on SBIR must be re-checked against the enacted 2026 text; INNOVATE Act-style provisions on foreign ties and repeat awardees may have been incorporated.

findings.title: SBIR ownership test: more than 50 percent owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or permanent residents
findings.detail: 13 CFR 121.702 requires an SBIR/STTR awardee to be a for-profit U.S. business (500 or fewer employees) that is more than 50 percent directly owned and controlled by one or more individuals who are citizens or permanent resident aliens of the United States, by other eligible small businesses, or (only where the agency elects) by multiple venture capital operating companies, hedge funds or private equity firms. Eligibility is self-certified and must exist at award.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase of 13 CFR 121.702(a): more than 50 percent directly owned and controlled by one or more individuals who are citizens of, or permanent resident aliens in, the United States.
findings.source_title: eCFR 13 CFR 121.702 What size and eligibility standards are applicable to the SBIR and STTR programs?
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: The Indonesian founder's shares never count in the numerator; the German founder's count only after the green card is issued. A 50/50 split fails the test; the German founder (post-PR) plus U.S.-citizen/PR holders must exceed 50 percent and hold control.

findings.title: SBIR foreign-affiliation disclosure form is mandatory; Germany and Indonesia are not 'foreign countries of concern'
findings.detail: The SBIR and STTR Extension Act of 2022 requires applicants to complete SBA's 'Required Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships to Foreign Countries' covering ownership, investment, foreign employment and talent-program ties. 'Foreign country of concern' is defined as the PRC, DPRK, Russia, Iran and any other country designated by the Secretary of State.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the term foreign country of concern means the People's Republic of China, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, the Russian Federation, the Islamic Republic of Iran, or any other country determined to be a country of concern by the Secretary of State.
findings.source_title: Required Disclosures of Foreign Affiliations or Relationships (SBIR.gov)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Both founders' foreign ties must be disclosed but neither nationality is a country of concern; the review risk is delay and questions, not an automatic bar, absent other ties.

findings.title: Agency due-diligence programs assess cybersecurity, patents, foreign ownership and employee affiliations; GAO finds gaps and DoD guidance pending
findings.detail: GAO-25-107402 and GAO-26-107972 report that all 11 participating agencies implemented due-diligence programs under the 2022 Extension Act, assessing four areas (cybersecurity practices, patents, foreign ownership, employee affiliations). As of August 2025 all agencies had incorporated only 3 of SBA's 12 best practices; as of January 2025 DoD planned updated guidance by 2026-06-30.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: as of August 2025, all agencies had incorporated three of the 12 best practices, such as leveraging standardized foreign affiliation disclosures.
findings.source_title: GAO-26-107972 Small Business Research Programs: Additional Actions Needed to Incorporate Best Practices for Addressing Foreign Risks; GAO-25-107402
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Expect inconsistent, component-specific vetting of the founders' foreign affiliations; keep clean documentation of ownership, funding sources and prior employment.

findings.title: Majority-VC-owned SBIR eligibility is agency-elective and poorly tracked (GAO-24-107004)
findings.detail: GAO-24-107004 found better data and clarity are needed on eligibility of venture-capital-owned businesses. The VCOC/hedge fund/PE ownership route exists only where an agency elects it and is capped in statute (RECALL: 25 percent of funds at NIH, DOE, NSF; 15 percent elsewhere). A cap table where investors collectively hold more than 50 percent can break eligibility.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase of GAO title: Better Data and Clarity on Eligibility of Venture Capital-Owned Businesses Are Needed.
findings.source_title: GAO-24-107004 Small Business Innovation Research: Better Data and Clarity on Eligibility of Venture Capital-Owned Businesses Are Needed
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: With only ~$250k of founder capital, a seed round could push citizen/PR ownership below 50 percent; sequencing of SBIR awards vs. dilution must be modeled.

findings.title: AFWERX Open Topic SBIR limits foreign-national participation to public-domain or fundamental research and requires all work in the U.S.
findings.detail: The AFWERX Ventures Open Topic Phase I FAQ (cleared AFRL-2025-3235, dated 2025-07-02) states that foreign-national participation under an award is limited to public-domain or fundamental research and that all work must be performed in the United States.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: it will limit the amount of foreign national participation allowed under the award to only public domain or fundamental research; all work must be done within the United States.
findings.source_title: AFWERX Open Topic Phase I Frequently Asked Questions (AFRL-2025-3235)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: A non-U.S.-person founder cannot be the technical lead on a DoD SBIR effort unless the work is structured as fundamental/public-domain research; whether DoD's 'foreign national' definition treats a permanent resident as a U.S. person must be confirmed per component.

findings.title: DoD SBIR BAA preface requires identification of foreign nationals and export-control compliance
findings.detail: The DoD SBIR 24.4 BAA preface (media.defense.gov) contains standard provisions on foreign national participation and export controls for proposals. RECALL (not re-read this session): DoD BAAs require offerors to identify all foreign nationals expected to work on the project, their countries of origin and visa status, and warn that ITAR/EAR may restrict their participation.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL - not re-verified this session: offerors must identify foreign nationals expected to be involved on the project and comply with ITAR/EAR.
findings.source_title: DoD SBIR 24.4 Preface
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Every DoD SBIR proposal will surface the Indonesian founder's status; plan the role split and technology control plan before proposing.

findings.title: CMMC DFARS clause effective 2025-11-10; Phase 1 self-assessments live; Phase 2 (C3PAO) transition suspended July 2026
findings.detail: DoD's 48 CFR CMMC rule was published 2025-09-10 and took effect 2025-11-10, adding DFARS 252.204-7021 (contract clause) and 252.204-7025 (solicitation provision making CMMC status a condition of award). Phase 1 (Level 1 and Level 2 self-assessment) runs 2025-11-10 to 2026-11-09. Phase 2 (Level 2 C3PAO certification, originally 2026-11-10) was suspended by DoD on 2026-07-13 pending a comprehensive review; no replacement dates announced.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: DoD suspended the transition to Phase 2 and future implementation milestones while it conducts a comprehensive review (July 13, 2026 suspension); no replacement dates announced.
findings.source_title: DoD Releases Final Rule Implementing CMMC Contract Clause (Cooley, 2025-09-25); CMMC Timeline 2026: Phase 2 Suspension (CMMC Command)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Near-term cost is a self-assessment and SPRS score, not a third-party audit; but any contract involving CUI still requires full NIST SP 800-171 implementation, and the suspension (secondary sources only) could be reversed.

findings.title: CMMC program rule (32 CFR Part 170) defines the three levels
findings.detail: RECALL - not re-verified this session: 32 CFR Part 170 was published 2024-10-15 and effective 2024-12-16. Level 1 = 15 FAR 52.204-21 safeguards (self); Level 2 = 110 NIST SP 800-171 Rev 2 controls (self or C3PAO depending on solicitation); Level 3 = 24 additional NIST SP 800-172 requirements assessed by DIBCAC. DoD uses Rev 2 via class deviation even though NIST published Rev 3 in May 2024.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: Level 2 aligns to the 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 Rev 2.
findings.source_title: eCFR 32 CFR Part 170 (Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Program)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Budget roughly a Level 2 self-assessment posture from day one if any DoD prototype will touch CUI; enclave-based scoping (e.g., GCC High or a managed enclave) is the usual startup approach.

findings.title: DFARS 252.204-7012 and 7019/7020 already impose NIST SP 800-171, 72-hour incident reporting and FedRAMP Moderate-equivalent cloud
findings.detail: RECALL - stable: DFARS 252.204-7012 requires adequate security per NIST SP 800-171 for covered defense information, cyber-incident reporting to DoD within 72 hours, and FedRAMP Moderate (or equivalent) for external cloud services handling CDI; 252.204-7019/7020 require a NIST SP 800-171 self-assessment score posted in SPRS. These clauses flow down to subcontractors and appear in many OT agreements by reference.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: contractor shall implement NIST SP 800-171 and report cyber incidents within 72 hours of discovery.
findings.source_title: DFARS 252.204-7012 Safeguarding Covered Defense Information and Cyber Incident Reporting
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Even before CMMC certification, the first CUI-bearing award triggers 7012; choose a cloud/enclave that satisfies FedRAMP Moderate equivalency.

findings.title: DoD Cloud Impact Levels (IL2/IL4/IL5/IL6) gate where C2 software can run
findings.detail: RECALL - stable: the DISA Cloud Computing Security Requirements Guide defines IL2 (public/non-CUI), IL4 (CUI), IL5 (higher-sensitivity CUI and NSS) and IL6 (SECRET). Commercial hyperscaler government regions hold IL4/IL5 provisional authorizations; startups usually start at IL2 or deploy through a platform partner (e.g., Platform One/Iron Bank, or a DevSecOps intermediary) to reach IL4/IL5, and only cleared entities operate at IL6.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: IL4 covers CUI; IL5 covers higher-sensitivity CUI and national security systems; IL6 covers classified information up to SECRET.
findings.source_title: DoD Cloud Computing Security Requirements Guide (DISA)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: An unclassified MVP can be demonstrated at IL2; operational C2 use typically needs IL4/IL5 hosting, which is achievable without clearances; IL6 requires cleared operators.

findings.title: ITAR treats a lawful permanent resident as a U.S. person (22 CFR 120.62)
findings.detail: Under 22 CFR 120.62 a 'U.S. person' includes a lawful permanent resident (8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(20)) or protected individual (8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3)), plus U.S.-incorporated entities. Foreign nationals on temporary status (F-1, OPT, H-1B, O-1, L-1, TN) are foreign persons regardless of residence duration and need DDTC authorization (typically DSP-5) to access ITAR technical data.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase of 22 CFR 120.62: U.S. person means a person who is a lawful permanent resident or a protected individual, and any corporation or entity incorporated to do business in the United States.
findings.source_title: eCFR 22 CFR 120.62 U.S. person
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: The German founder's export-control exposure ends at green-card issuance; the Indonesian founder's persists until permanent residence, so ITAR-touching work must be walled off or licensed.

findings.title: ITAR USML targeted revisions (IFR 2025-01-17, effective 2025-09-15) revised definitions and Category XI
findings.detail: DDTC's interim final rule (Federal Register document 2025-01313) amended 22 CFR 121.0 and 121.1, revised USML definitions and Categories II, IV, V, VII-XIV and XIX-XXI, with amendments effective 2025-09-15; Category XI (military electronics) was revised so that certain anti-jam antennas no longer provide a critical military advantage given commercial GPS-resiliency use.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: USML Category XI was revised to reflect that certain anti-jam antennas no longer provide a critical military advantage.
findings.source_title: Federal Register: International Traffic in Arms Regulations: U.S. Munitions List Targeted Revisions
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Category XI wording as of 2025-09-15 is the controlling text for any C2 hardware/electronics adjacency; classification analysis must use the revised list.

findings.title: DDTC's redefinition of 'defense services' is proposed and a final rule sits on the regulatory agenda
findings.detail: DDTC proposed revising the ITAR definition of 'defense services' (22 CFR 120.32) and adding controls on assistance to foreign militaries and intelligence activities (RECALL: proposed rule published mid-2024). Trade press (WTTL) and Lexology/Thompson Hine coverage report a final rule on the Unified Agenda; no final rule confirmed this session.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: DDTC's Unified Agenda lists a final rule redefining defense services as part of planned initiatives.
findings.source_title: DDTC Issues Proposed Rule Revising ITAR Definition and Controls related to Defense Services (Baker McKenzie); DDTC Expands ITAR Controls, Sets Aggressive Regulatory Agenda (WTTL)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Even EAR99 software can generate an ITAR 'defense service' when the company trains or integrates it for a foreign military (e.g., Bundeswehr or TNI); allied go-to-market needs a TAA/DSP-5 analysis.

findings.title: What makes C2 software ITAR: 'specially designed' for a USML article, not military end use alone
findings.detail: INFERENCE from the regulatory structure: software is ITAR technical data when it is 'specially designed' (22 CFR 120.41 catch-and-release) for a defense article (e.g., fire control under Category XII, intelligence systems under XI(b), EW under XI(a)). Generic C2/COP/data-fabric software built from commercial components that also serves civil users generally falls under the EAR (EAR99, or 5D002 if it implements non-standard cryptography), or 600-series (e.g., 9D610, 3D611) if specially designed for a 600-series military item. The 2014 ECR moved military computers and many electronics from USML XI to ECCN 3A611. Jurisdiction is settled by a Commodity Jurisdiction request to DDTC or a CCATS to BIS.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (Military Embedded Systems): the Category XI revision transferred control of military computers from the USML to Commerce under ECCN 3A611.
findings.source_title: Proposed revision to USML military electronics (Military Embedded Systems); DDTC ITAR landing page
findings.label: INFERENCE
findings.startup_relevance: Product architecture is a compliance lever: keep the core generic and commercially deployable, isolate military-specific adapters (Link 16, fire control, specific sensors) as separable modules that may be ITAR/600-series and built by U.S. persons.

findings.title: EAR deemed-export rule: license needed to release controlled technology to a foreign national when a license would be needed for that country
findings.detail: BIS treats release of controlled technology or source code to a foreign person in the U.S. as an export to that person's most recent country of citizenship or permanent residency (15 CFR 734.13(b)); lawful permanent residents and protected individuals are excluded. A license is required only if a license would be required to export to the home country. BIS publishes Guidelines for Foreign National License Applications; employers sponsoring H-1B/L-1/O-1 workers must attest on USCIS Form I-129 whether a deemed-export license is required. RECALL: Indonesia is in Country Group B (not D:1/D:5), so EAR99 technology needs no license, but NS Column 1 items including 600-series technology require a license to Indonesia and thus a deemed-export license for an Indonesian national.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (BIS): licenses are required for release of controlled technology or software to a foreign national only if a license is required for the export of such items to the home country.
findings.source_title: What is a deemed export? (BIS); Guidelines for Foreign National License Applications (BIS)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: For an EAR99 product the Indonesian founder is unconstrained; once 600-series technology (military UAS, military electronics) enters the codebase, a BIS deemed-export license (weeks to months) or a technology control plan is needed, and the I-129 attestation becomes material.

findings.title: ITAR has no deemed-export license exception for domestic foreign-person employees; DSP-5 or a TAA is needed
findings.detail: Foreign-person employees in the U.S. need prior DDTC authorization (typically a DSP-5 license naming the employee and technical data) before accessing ITAR technical data; the 22 CFR 126.18 exemption applies to foreign employees of foreign licensees abroad, not to a U.S. startup's domestic staff. Indonesia is not a 22 CFR 126.1 proscribed destination, so licensing is possible but discretionary and program-specific.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (industry guidance): foreign nationals who do not qualify as U.S. persons need prior authorization, typically a DSP-5 license filed through DDTC's DECCS portal.
findings.source_title: ITAR Non-US Persons: Green Card and Deemed Export Rules (Lenzo); DDTC Understand the ITAR
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Any ITAR-touching segment implies the Indonesian founder is excluded from that technical data until licensed; the company would also need to register with DDTC (22 CFR 122) and run a TCP.

findings.title: FOCI under 32 CFR 117.11: any non-citizen, including a permanent resident, is a 'foreign interest'; mitigation instruments are graduated
findings.detail: A facility clearance requires FOCI to be negated or mitigated. 32 CFR 117.11 lists instruments in increasing restrictiveness: Board Resolution, Security Control Agreement, Special Security Agreement, Voting Trust or Proxy Agreement. DCSA evaluates FOCI with the SF-328 (updated 2025-05-01). RECALL: the NISP definition of 'foreign interest' includes any person who is not a citizen or national of the United States, so both founders (even after the German founder's green card) count as foreign interests as owners, officers or directors until naturalization.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase of 32 CFR 117.11(d)(2): methods include Board Resolution, Security Control Agreement, Special Security Agreement, Voting Trust or Proxy Agreement, or any combination.
findings.source_title: eCFR 32 CFR 117.11 Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence (FOCI); Understanding FOCI (ISI Defense)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: A facility clearance is not impossible but would require cleared U.S.-citizen key management personnel, a sponsoring contract, and FOCI mitigation that may sideline the founders from classified matters; foreign investors compound the FOCI picture.

findings.title: DoDI 5205.87 extends FOCI risk mitigation to certain unclassified DoD contracts
findings.detail: DoD Instruction 5205.87 'Mitigating Risks Related to Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence for DoD Contracts' implements FY2020 NDAA Section 847 beneficial-ownership assessment for covered contracts (RECALL: contracts over $5 million involving CUI, personnel security, or sensitive work). It signals that FOCI scrutiny is not confined to classified work.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Title paraphrase: Mitigating Risks Related to Foreign Ownership, Control, or Influence for DoD Contracts.
findings.source_title: DoD Instruction 5205.87
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: As contracts grow past prototype scale, beneficial-ownership disclosure and FOCI assessment will surface the foreign founders and any foreign investors even without a clearance requirement.

findings.title: Personnel security clearances require U.S. citizenship; both founders are years from eligibility
findings.detail: RECALL - stable: EO 12968 and SEAD 4 limit personnel clearances to U.S. citizens; a Limited Access Authorization for non-citizens is rare, limited to Secret/Confidential with a compelling need, and does not create an FCL-eligible KMP. Naturalization typically requires five years of permanent residence (three if married to a citizen), so the German founder would be clearance-eligible only in roughly 2031-2032 at the earliest and the Indonesian founder later still.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: only U.S. citizens are eligible for a security clearance; LAAs for non-U.S. citizens are exceptional.
findings.source_title: Executive Order 12968; SEAD 4 (ODNI); 32 CFR Part 117 (DCSA)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Classified-dependent business models require hiring cleared U.S.-citizen executives/engineers and accepting that founders cannot see classified requirements, test results or deployment data for most of a decade.

findings.title: OTA/CSO route has no statutory U.S.-ownership test; nontraditional defense contractor status is about CAS coverage, not nationality
findings.detail: 10 U.S.C. 3014 defines a nontraditional defense contractor as an entity that has not performed, for at least one year before solicitation, any DoD contract subject to full Cost Accounting Standards coverage. 10 U.S.C. 4022 prototype OTs require a nontraditional participant to a significant extent, all-small-business participation, one-third cost share, or exceptional circumstances (RECALL for 4022 conditions). DIU's commercial page states any individual or commercial entity may respond to its solicitations; the DIU CSO (HQ0845-20-S-C001) requires compliance with export-control laws. Individual solicitations may add U.S.-person, CUI or clearance requirements.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase of 10 U.S.C. 3014: an entity that is not currently performing and has not performed, for at least the one-year period preceding the solicitation, any DoD contract or subcontract subject to full coverage under the cost accounting standards.
findings.source_title: 10 USC 3014 Nontraditional defense contractor (uscode.house.gov); DIU Commercial Solutions Opening (sam.gov); An Offeror's Legal Guide to CSOs (Holland & Knight, 2026-03)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: OT prototypes (DIU, Army, AFWERX non-SBIR, SOCOM) are the most accessible federal vehicle for this team; the constraint moves from ownership to what the solicitation says about CUI, ITAR and foreign nationals.

findings.title: GAO-25-106856 documents DIU's expanded role and measurement gaps
findings.detail: GAO's 2025 report on DIU (GAO-25-106856) recommends actions to assess progress and enhance collaboration as DIU scales its commercial-solutions role; DIU markets access to a '$100+ billion market' to commercial firms. Contents not read in detail this session.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Title paraphrase: Defense Innovation Unit: Actions Needed to Assess Progress and Further Enhance Collaboration.
findings.source_title: GAO-25-106856 (PDF); DIU Work With Us - Commercial
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: DIU remains the principal commercial-entry door; GAO's critique implies transition-to-production metrics are still immature, so prototype awards should not be read as scaled demand.

findings.title: Fundamental research exclusion protects university work, not the startup's product development
findings.detail: RECALL - stable: ITAR 22 CFR 120.34(a)(8) and EAR 15 CFR 734.8 exclude information arising from fundamental research at accredited U.S. institutions of higher learning that is ordinarily published and not subject to access or dissemination restrictions. Corporate development of a product, or university work under a DoD agreement with publication/foreign-national restrictions, does not qualify.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: fundamental research means basic and applied research in science and engineering where the resulting information is ordinarily published and shared broadly.
findings.source_title: 22 CFR 120.34 Public domain; 15 CFR 734.8 Technology or software that arises during, or results from, fundamental research
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Student founders can prototype algorithms (fusion, PED models) under university fundamental research with both founders participating, but that protection ends when the work moves into the company or takes DoD-restricted funding.

findings.title: ATAK-CIV and its SDK are open-sourced government-owned software with a plugin architecture; TAK-GOV/MIL remain distribution-controlled
findings.detail: The TAK Configuration Steering Board open-sourced ATAK-CIV and the SDK on DoD GitHub (deptofdefense/AndroidTacticalAssaultKit-CIV; TAK-Product-Center/atak-civ) and approved public release of additional binaries on TAK.gov to support IRAD development. ATAK's plugin architecture lets third parties add mission-specific capability; the TAK software license agreement between the U.S. Government (Army CCDC C5ISR Center) and the recipient governs TAK-CIV, TAK-GOV, TAK-MIL and the SDK. Government-user plugin distribution runs through TAK.gov processes and plugin signing.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase: the TAK Configuration Steering Board has open sourced ATAK-CIV and SDK on DoD GitHub and approved the public release of additional binaries on TAK.gov to support IRAD development.
findings.source_title: TAK Product Center on GitHub; AndroidTacticalAssaultKit-CIV (deptofdefense GitHub); TAK.gov Our Process
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Lowest-friction unclassified entry: both founders can build ATAK-CIV plugins and TAK Server integrations today; the license terms (and any copyleft obligations) and the TAK.gov review path for military users need counsel review before commercialization.

findings.title: Citizenship-based hiring restrictions must be tied to an actual legal requirement (8 U.S.C. 1324b)
findings.detail: DOJ's Immigrant and Employee Rights Section enforces 8 U.S.C. 1324b; employers may not impose blanket 'U.S. citizens only' rules or misapply export-control requirements as a pretext for citizenship or national-origin discrimination. Restrictions are lawful only where required by law, regulation, executive order or government contract.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Paraphrase (Greenberg Traurig): IER guidance warns against using export-control compliance as a basis for citizenship-status discrimination unless required by law.
findings.source_title: Immigrant and Employee Rights at the Department of Justice - National Origin and Citizenship Discrimination (Greenberg Traurig Inside Business Immigration)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Ironically relevant to this team: when it later hires cleared or U.S.-person-only roles, job postings and screening must be worded around the specific ITAR/clearance requirement.

findings.title: CFIUS mandatory declarations can be triggered by foreign investment in a startup whose products are ITAR/600-series 'critical technologies'
findings.detail: RECALL - not re-verified this session: under 31 CFR 800.401 a mandatory CFIUS declaration applies when a foreign person acquires control of, or a covered investment (board seat, observer, access to material nonpublic technical information, or involvement in substantive decisions) in, a 'TID U.S. business' producing critical technologies (including USML and 600-series items) for which a U.S. regulatory authorization would be required to export to that investor's country. Excepted investors (Australia, Canada, New Zealand, UK, subject to conditions) are exempt; German, Indonesian or Singaporean investors are not.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: mandatory declaration for covered transactions involving TID U.S. businesses producing critical technologies where an export authorization would be required.
findings.source_title: 31 CFR Part 800 (CFIUS regulations)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: If the product becomes export-controlled, a German or Indonesian angel/VC taking a board seat or information rights could require a CFIUS filing; keeping the core EAR99 preserves fundraising flexibility.

findings.title: 2025 software acquisition reforms push DoD toward CSOs/OTs for software, widening non-SBIR entry
findings.detail: RECALL - not re-read this session: the Secretary of Defense's 2025-03-06 memorandum directed the Software Acquisition Pathway with CSOs and OTs as the default for software, and EO 14265 (2025-04-09) called for prioritizing commercial solutions and OT use. DIU's page 'Advancing DoD operational capabilities with software acquisition reform' describes DIU's role in that shift.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: directs use of the Software Acquisition Pathway and Commercial Solutions Openings and Other Transactions as default for software acquisition.
findings.source_title: Advancing DoD Operational Capabilities with Software Acquisition Reform (DIU)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: The vehicle least sensitive to the founders' nationality (OT/CSO) is the one DoD is expanding for software; this partially offsets the SBIR ownership problem.

findings.title: ITAR registration (22 CFR Part 122) is required once the company manufactures defense articles or furnishes defense services and discloses foreign ownership/control
findings.detail: RECALL - stable: any U.S. person who manufactures, exports or brokers defense articles or furnishes defense services must register with DDTC (annual fee), and the registration statement requires disclosure of foreign ownership or control (thresholds in 22 CFR 122.2(b)). Registration is not conditioned on U.S. ownership but foreign-controlled registrants receive greater scrutiny and must update DDTC on changes.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: registration statement must disclose whether the registrant is owned or controlled by foreign persons.
findings.source_title: 22 CFR Part 122 Registration of Manufacturers and Exporters (DDTC)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: A decision to build ITAR modules triggers registration cost and disclosure of the founders' nationality and any foreign investors; an EAR-only product avoids it.

findings.title: CUI access by foreign nationals is permitted only when consistent with export controls and the contract; export-controlled CUI is effectively U.S.-person-only
findings.detail: RECALL - not re-verified this session: DoDI 5200.48 and 32 CFR Part 2002 allow contractor foreign nationals to access CUI for a lawful government purpose when not prohibited by law, export controls or the contract; CUI marked export-controlled (EXPT) or CTI derived from ITAR/EAR-controlled data cannot be released to a foreign person without authorization. Most C2 integration data (ICDs, network diagrams, sensor specs) is CUI and often export-controlled.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: access to CUI by foreign nationals must be consistent with export control laws, contract requirements and the lawful government purpose standard.
findings.source_title: DoDI 5200.48 Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI); 32 CFR Part 2002
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Even unclassified DoD prototype work will hand the company CUI; the Indonesian founder's access must be governed by contract terms and export-control markings, which favors a U.S.-person-led integration role and a foreign-national-accessible core product.

findings.title: NIH's 2023 implementation notice shows how foreign-disclosure requirements operate pre- and post-award
findings.detail: The Federal Register notice of 2023-06-16 implemented NIH's SBIR/STTR foreign disclosure pre-award and post-award requirements, illustrating the agency-level operationalization of the 2022 Act (disclosure at application, updates during performance, potential rejection or termination for undisclosed covered relationships). DoD components have adopted analogous processes (GAO-24-106400).
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: Title paraphrase: Implementation of the NIH SBIR and STTR Foreign Disclosure Pre-Award and Post-Award Requirements.
findings.source_title: Federal Register: Implementation of the NIH SBIR and STTR Foreign Disclosure Pre-Award and Post-Award Requirements
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Disclosure obligations continue after award; changes in the founders' status, foreign funding or foreign employment must be reported during performance.

findings.title: Encryption in a commercial C2 product is usually 5D002 with License Exception ENC; open-source crypto source needs only notification
findings.detail: RECALL - stable: software implementing non-standard cryptography or exceeding mass-market thresholds is ECCN 5D002; most commercial C2/SA software qualifies for License Exception ENC after self-classification or a CCATS, and publicly available open-source encryption source code is released under 15 CFR 742.15(b) with an email notification. Indonesia is not in Country Group E:1, so ENC generally covers exports and deemed exports to an Indonesian national.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: License Exception ENC authorizes export of most 5D002 items to non-E:1 destinations after classification or notification.
findings.source_title: 15 CFR 740.17 License Exception ENC; 15 CFR 742.15 (BIS)
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: Encryption is not the blocker for this team; a one-time classification/notification step suffices for an EAR-only product with TLS, X.509 or standard crypto (as used by TAK).

findings.title: SBIR data rights (20-year protection) and OT-negotiated IP allow an unclassified commercial core with government-funded adapters
findings.detail: RECALL - stable: DFARS 252.227-7018 protects SBIR-developed data for 20 years from award, with government-purpose rights thereafter; under OTs (10 U.S.C. 4022) IP and data rights are negotiated and commercial-item terms are common. This supports an architecture in which the commercial core stays company-owned and government-funded plugins/adapters are delivered with negotiated rights.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: SBIR data rights period is 20 years from award for data generated under the award.
findings.source_title: DFARS 252.227-7018 Rights in Noncommercial Technical Data and Computer Software - SBIR Program
findings.label: FACT
findings.startup_relevance: IP structure and export structure can be aligned: commercial core (EAR99, foreign-founder-accessible, company-owned) plus controlled adapters (U.S.-person-built, government-rights-negotiated).

findings.title: Allied vehicles (NATO DIANA, German innovation channels) are open to the German founder but EU-only instruments are constrained by third-country control
findings.detail: RECALL - not verified this session: NATO DIANA accelerator eligibility extends to companies established in NATO member states (Germany and the U.S. both qualify) without a citizenship test comparable to SBIR; German national channels (Cyber Innovation Hub der Bundeswehr, BAAINBw procurement, SPRIND) are open to German-based entities; EU European Defence Fund grants require EU-established entities not controlled by third countries, which a U.S.-incorporated company with an Indonesian co-founder would not satisfy without an EU subsidiary and control arrangements.
findings.quote_or_paraphrase: RECALL: DIANA calls are open to innovators from NATO Allied nations; EDF requires entities established in the EU and not controlled by third countries.
findings.source_title: NATO DIANA; European Defence Fund eligibility (European Commission)
findings.label: HYPOTHESIS
findings.startup_relevance: The German founder gives optionality in NATO/German channels (coalition interoperability, TAK-adjacent SA), but a dual-jurisdiction structure raises its own export (ITAR defense services, German AWG/BAFA) and control questions.

structured.segment_taxonomy_note: Segment IDs S01-S14 below use assumed labels derived from the study brief (C2/battle management, tactical comms/DDIL, data fabric, sensor fusion/track management, ISR PED, dismounted SA/TAK, space C2, EW/EMSO, cyber/ZT/CDS, M&S/training, edge compute/DevSecOps, coalition/MPE, autonomy/C-UAS C2, decision support/targeting). Reconcile with the master taxonomy before merging; the regulatory judgments attach to the described function, not the ID.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Mission command / C2 and battle management software (COP)
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: EAR99 or 5D002 if generic; ITAR/600-series only if specially designed for a USML system (fire control, intelligence system)
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: ATAK-CIV/TAK Server, Cursor-on-Target, MIL-STD-2525/APP-6 symbology (public), OGC standards, public-safety and emergency-management COP market, exercise/experimentation events (unclassified enclaves)
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: CUI in ICDs and network data; operational C2 runs at IL5/SECRET; NGC2-class integration eventually classified; DFARS 7012/CMMC L2
regulatory_matrix.notes: Founder-friendly core; military adapters should be modular and U.S.-person-built.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Tactical communications, networking and DDIL data transport
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: 5A002/5D002 for encrypted transport; ITAR XI(a) or 600-series for military radios/waveforms; Type 1/COMSEC classified and NSA-controlled
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: Commercial MANET radios, Starlink/commercial SATCOM, open mesh stacks (batman-adv, Meshtastic), DTN Bundle Protocol (RFC 9171), SDR/GNU Radio
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Waveform and radio-specific software tends to be controlled; COMSEC excluded; spectrum authorizations
regulatory_matrix.notes: Software-only store-and-forward/sync layers over commercial links are the accessible slice.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Data fabric / data mesh / integration and API translation
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: Apache NiFi/Kafka, OGC/NIEM/CoT, unclassified STANAG profiles, NATO FMN spiral specifications (public), commercial data catalogs; MPE unclassified environments
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Real schemas/ICDs are CUI and often export-controlled; cross-domain movement is a CDS (classified) problem
regulatory_matrix.notes: Strong fit for foreign-founder-accessible core; value depends on access to real message formats.

regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: EAR99 for generic trackers; becomes 600-series/ITAR technical data when tuned to military sensor performance, Link 16/J-series or threat libraries
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: ADS-B, AIS, commercial radar/EO/IR feeds, open-source tracking frameworks (e.g., Stone Soup, FilterPy), synthetic scenarios
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Sensor performance data and threat parameters are classified; Link 16 access requires government sponsorship; algorithms on classified data become classified
regulatory_matrix.notes: University fundamental research is a legitimate incubator for algorithms before company formation.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: ISR processing, exploitation and dissemination (imagery/OSINT; SIGINT separately)
regulatory_matrix.mvp_unclassified_commercial: yes for commercial imagery and OSINT; no for SIGINT
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: EAR99 for commercial-imagery analytics; models trained on classified data become classified
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: Commercial EO/SAR providers, public datasets (xView, SpaceNet), NGA commercial pathways, CDAO Tradewinds marketplace
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: NGA/NRO/NSA data classified; CUI/PII handling; ITAR for satellite-specific tasking software
regulatory_matrix.notes: Commercial imagery PED is one of the cleanest unclassified wedges.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Dismounted situational awareness / TAK ecosystem and plugins
regulatory_matrix.classification_dependence: none for civil/public-safety plugins; eventually for military-only features
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: EAR99/5D002 for ATAK-CIV plugins; plugins interfacing to fires, Link 16 or specific military radios may be ITAR
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: ATAK-CIV source and SDK (DoD GitHub), TAK Server, TAK.gov third-party plugin process, DHS/first-responder TAK community
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: TAK software license terms; TAK-GOV/MIL builds distribution-restricted; plugin signing and TPC review for government users
regulatory_matrix.notes: Best immediate fit for this founding team.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Space domain C2, SATCOM management and space data
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: 9x515/USML XV for satellite and ground-control specifics; EAR99 for commercial SATCOM management analytics
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: Public TLE/space-track data, commercial SDA providers, Unified Data Library unclassified tier (approval required), Space Force Commercial Space Office
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: National security space data classified; ITAR XV touches ground systems; USSF programs at high IL
regulatory_matrix.notes: Public evidence insufficient on unclassified USSF on-ramps beyond commercial data programs.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Electronic warfare / EMSO and spectrum management
regulatory_matrix.classification_dependence: immediate for effects/techniques; eventually for spectrum planning
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: ITAR XI(a)/(b) likely once tied to military EW; commercial spectrum tools EAR99/5A001
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: GNU Radio, commercial SDR monitoring, NTIA/FCC spectrum datasets, EMS planning with unclassified emitter data
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Techniques, emitter libraries and effects are classified; Indonesian founder excluded from ITAR data
regulatory_matrix.notes: Inherently controlled; poor fit for this team's first product.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Cyber, zero trust/ICAM and cross-domain solutions
regulatory_matrix.mvp_unclassified_commercial: yes for ZT/ICAM/DevSecOps security; no for CDS
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: NIST SP 800-207, DoD ZT Strategy and overlays, Platform One/Iron Bank hardening, commercial IdP integrations
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: CDS requires NCDSMO/NSA Raise-the-Bar assessment and classified testing; FedRAMP/IL authorizations
regulatory_matrix.notes: ZT tooling is commercial-first; CDS is a cleared-vendor market.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Modeling, simulation, training and C2 digital twins
regulatory_matrix.classification_dependence: none for unclassified training; eventually for real threat/order-of-battle data
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: EAR99 for generic wargaming/training; USML IX for simulators specially designed for USML articles
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: Unreal/Unity, DIS/HLA standards (IEEE 1278/1516), open terrain data, commercial serious-games vendors, unclassified doctrine
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Government models (e.g., OneSAF) restricted; classified threat models
regulatory_matrix.notes: Good sandbox for C2 decision-support concepts without controlled data.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Edge compute, tactical cloud and DevSecOps platforms
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: Kubernetes/K3s, Platform One Big Bang (open source), Iron Bank, hyperscaler government regions and edge appliances, ruggedized COTS
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: IL4/IL5 authorization, CMMC when CUI hosted, hardware supply-chain rules (Section 889 and NDAA component bans) if selling hardware

regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: Software EAR99, but assistance to foreign militaries can be an ITAR defense service; National Disclosure Policy governs releasability
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: NATO FMN spiral specs, public STANAGs, TAK coalition use, NATO DIANA, unclassified interoperability sandboxes; CWIX/Bold Quest by invitation
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Defense services redefinition pending; foreign disclosure rules; FMS/DCS channels
regulatory_matrix.notes: German founder's NATO ties are an asset; the Indonesian nexus needs care given TAA/DSP-5 requirements.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Autonomy / uncrewed systems C2 and counter-UAS integration
regulatory_matrix.mvp_unclassified_commercial: yes for commercial-drone C2 and detection
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: 600-series (9D610) once specially designed for military UAS; EAR99 for commercial-drone tooling (MAVLink/PX4/ArduPilot); C-UAS mitigation authority limited to federal entities
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: Open-source autopilots/protocols, Blue UAS framework and DIU CSOs, commercial RF/radar detection sensors
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Deemed export of 600-series technology to the Indonesian founder needs a BIS license; kinetic/EW mitigation is controlled and legally restricted
regulatory_matrix.notes: Detection and C2 of commercial drones is accessible; military UAS integration is not.

regulatory_matrix.assumed_segment_label: Decision support, AI planning, wargaming and targeting support
regulatory_matrix.likely_export_status_of_mvp: EAR99 for planning/logistics decision support; ITAR XII fire-control for weaponeering/targeting
regulatory_matrix.commercial_unclassified_starting_points: CDAO Tradewinds, unclassified doctrine and open logistics data, commercial LLM/agent stacks, M&S sandboxes
regulatory_matrix.primary_constraints: Targeting chains run at SECRET (e.g., Maven-class systems); AI on classified data classified; responsible-AI and IL5 hosting requirements
regulatory_matrix.notes: Split: logistics/mission-planning decision support is accessible; targeting is not.

founder_analysis.assumptions: German founder is expected to become a lawful permanent resident (date unknown); Indonesian founder is assumed to remain a non-U.S. person (temporary status or abroad); company assumed to be a U.S. (Delaware) C-corporation. Statements are business-level descriptions of constraints, not legal conclusions.

sbir_sttr_eligibility.constraint: 13 CFR 121.702 requires more than 50 percent direct ownership and control by U.S. citizens/permanent residents (or eligible small businesses/elective VC route). Eligibility is assessed at award and self-certified; misrepresentation carries fraud exposure (GAO-24-105470).
sbir_sttr_eligibility.team_implication: Until the German founder holds a green card, neither founder's equity counts, so the company is ineligible unless U.S. citizens/PRs hold a controlling majority. After the green card, the German founder plus any citizen/PR holders must exceed 50 percent and hold control (board, voting). The Indonesian founder's stake caps the foreign-owned share; options and convertible instruments are treated as exercised under SBA affiliation rules (13 CFR 121.103). DoD components additionally restrict foreign-national technical participation (AFWERX FAQ 2025-07-02), which may bar the Indonesian founder from being PI or performing core R&D on SBIR-funded work even if the company is eligible.
open_questions: Does DoD's SBIR 'foreign national' definition treat a permanent resident as a U.S. person (component-specific)?
Did S. 3971 change the ownership test, foreign-ties bars or repeat-award limits?
Can the Indonesian founder hold non-voting equity without triggering 'control' findings?
Timing: when does the German founder's PR status vest relative to solicitation cycles?
sbir_sttr_eligibility.label: INFERENCE

diu_ota_eligibility.constraint: 10 U.S.C. 4022 and 3014 impose no citizenship or ownership test; DIU states any individual or commercial entity may respond. Individual CSOs/OT agreements can require U.S.-person performance, CUI safeguards, ITAR compliance, and eventual facility clearance; agreements officers retain discretion.
diu_ota_eligibility.team_implication: The most accessible federal vehicle for this team. Nontraditional status is automatic for a new company. Risk shifts to solicitation-level terms: if the project involves export-controlled technical data or CUI, the Indonesian founder's role must be structured. Cost-share or all-small-business conditions are easy to meet.
open_questions: Do current DIU/Army/AFWERX CSO templates include foreign-national or U.S.-ownership clauses for C2 topics?
How do agreements officers treat a non-U.S.-person co-founder with source-code access?
diu_ota_eligibility.label: INFERENCE

deemed_export_exposure.constraint: EAR 734.13(b) and ITAR 120.62/120.63: releasing controlled technology/source code to a foreign person in the U.S. is an export to their country. LPRs are U.S. persons under both regimes. Indonesia (Country Group B, RECALL) requires licenses for NS1 items including 600-series technology; EAR99 requires none. ITAR technical data needs a DSP-5/TAA for any foreign person, with no domestic-employee exception.
deemed_export_exposure.team_implication: Pre-green-card, both founders are foreign persons; post-green-card only the Indonesian founder is. An EAR99/5D002 commercial core imposes essentially no friction on the Indonesian founder. Any ITAR or 600-series module requires a technology control plan segregating repositories, systems and meetings, plus licensing (BIS deemed-export license; DDTC DSP-5) before access. Sponsoring the Indonesian founder on H-1B/O-1 requires the I-129 deemed-export attestation. If the Indonesian founder works from Indonesia, the same classification analysis governs cross-border transfers, and cloud-hosting of controlled data must be U.S.-person-restricted.
open_questions: Product-level classification (CJ/CCATS) of the planned MVP
Whether any planned government data (ICDs, sensor specs) is export-controlled CUI
Feasibility and timeline of a DSP-5 for an Indonesian national on a specific program
deemed_export_exposure.label: INFERENCE

clearance_dependent_models.constraint: Personnel clearances require U.S. citizenship; facility clearances require cleared U.S.-citizen KMP, a sponsoring contract, and FOCI negation/mitigation. NISP treats any non-citizen (including LPRs) as a foreign interest.
clearance_dependent_models.team_implication: Any model that requires the founders to see classified requirements, data or deployments is unavailable for roughly 5-8 years (naturalization timelines). Workarounds: (a) unclassified product + cleared integrator/prime deploys at IL6; (b) hire a cleared U.S.-citizen SMO/FSO and pursue an FCL with FOCI mitigation (Board Resolution or SCA if founders' influence is limited; SSA/proxy if they control), accepting exclusion from classified matters; (c) partner with FFRDC/UARC or cleared consultants for classified testing. Each dilutes founder control over the classified part of the business.
open_questions: Would DCSA accept a Board Resolution/SCA where both founders are officers and majority owners?
Which prime or program office would sponsor an FCL?
Board composition needed to mitigate founder FOCI
clearance_dependent_models.label: INFERENCE

foci_risk_at_fundraising.constraint: 32 CFR 117.11 and SF-328 assess foreign ownership (including minority stakes), foreign board members/KMP, foreign debt, and foreign revenue/contracts. DoDI 5205.87 extends beneficial-ownership scrutiny to certain unclassified contracts. CFIUS mandatory filings can apply to non-excepted foreign investors in a critical-technology startup.
foci_risk_at_fundraising.team_implication: German or Indonesian angels, family offices, European VCs or Singapore/Indonesian sovereign-linked funds add FOCI factors on top of the founders' own status; U.S. VCs with foreign LPs are generally acceptable but funds controlled from abroad are not. If the product becomes ITAR/600-series, a foreign investor with a board seat, observer rights or technical information access may trigger a CFIUS declaration. Excepted-investor status (AU/CA/NZ/UK) is more benign than German or Indonesian capital.
open_questions: Investor nationality/control mapping for the seed round
Whether to grant information/board rights to non-U.S. investors
Whether the product will be a critical technology at the time of investment
foci_risk_at_fundraising.label: INFERENCE

cap_table_structuring_questions: Target ownership split so that U.S. citizens/PRs (German founder post-PR, U.S. hires, U.S. investors) hold more than 50 percent and control, if SBIR is in the plan; model dilution scenarios against 13 CFR 121.702 and 121.103 (options/notes counted as exercised).
Whether the Indonesian founder should hold voting or non-voting stock, and how 'control' (board seats, protective provisions) is analyzed by SBA and DCSA.
Timing of German founder's PR status relative to first SBIR self-certification; what happens if PR is delayed.
Investor screening: excepted vs non-excepted foreign investors; information and board rights; CFIUS mandatory-declaration analysis if critical technology.
KMP design for a future FCL: a cleared U.S.-citizen CEO or SMO and FSO; founder titles and authorities; board composition with outside U.S.-citizen directors.
Beneficial-ownership disclosure readiness (SAM.gov, FAR 52.204-7 and 847 regime) and ITAR 122.2 foreign ownership disclosures.
Whether an EU/German subsidiary is needed for NATO/German channels and how control would flow without triggering U.S. FOCI or ITAR defense-service issues.
Founder vesting and IP assignment executed before any government funding; SBIR data rights and OT IP terms aligned with the commercial-core/adapter split.

timeline_view.now_to_pr: Both founders foreign persons; OT/CSO, university research, TAK plugins, public-safety COP and commercial imagery PED viable; SBIR not viable; no ITAR/600-series data in company.
timeline_view.post_pr_german_founder: German founder is a U.S. person for ITAR/EAR and counts for SBIR ownership; still a foreign interest for FOCI and ineligible for clearance. SBIR viable if majority test met; controlled modules can be built by the German founder and U.S. staff behind a TCP.
timeline_view.post_naturalization_(approx_5y_after_pr): German founder clearance-eligible; FCL path becomes realistic with FOCI mitigation for remaining foreign ownership (Indonesian founder, foreign investors).
timeline_view.label: INFERENCE

specialist_counsel_review_list: Export-control jurisdiction and classification of the planned MVP and each adapter (Commodity Jurisdiction request to DDTC and/or CCATS to BIS), including 22 CFR 120.41 'specially designed' analysis and encryption classification (5D002/ENC/742.15(b)).
Technology Control Plan design: repository, cloud, device and meeting segregation for the Indonesian founder; remote-work location and data-residency rules; I-129 deemed-export attestation.
Deemed-export licensing strategy: BIS license feasibility for an Indonesian national for 600-series technology; DDTC DSP-5/TAA feasibility for ITAR data; timelines and conditions.

ITAR registration timing (22 CFR 122) and foreign ownership/control disclosures; whether furnishing integration/training to allied militaries constitutes a defense service under current and pending 120.32 definitions.

SBIR/STTR eligibility computation under 13 CFR 121.702/121.103 (ownership, control, affiliation, options/notes), timing of the German founder's PR status, and whether the 2026 reauthorization changed eligibility or foreign-ties rules.
DoD component definitions of 'foreign national' for SBIR/OT participation and whether a PR is treated as a U.S. person; permissible roles for the Indonesian founder on funded work.
SBIR foreign-affiliation disclosure completeness (both founders' education, employment, funding, talent programs) and post-award update obligations.
FOCI analysis under 32 CFR 117.11 and SF-328: founder status, investor mix, board design, KMP plan; realistic mitigation instrument and FCL sponsorship path; DoDI 5205.87/Section 847 disclosures.
CFIUS analysis for each non-U.S. investor (control, covered investment rights, excepted-investor status, critical-technology status of the business).

CUI handling: DFARS 252.204-7012 applicability, NIST SP 800-171 scoping, SPRS score, CMMC level required by target solicitations, cloud FedRAMP Moderate equivalency, and foreign-national access to CUI under DoDI 5200.48.
OT/CSO agreement terms: IP and data rights, foreign-national clauses, follow-on production expectations, cost-share treatment, flow-down of 7012.
TAK software license agreement and any copyleft terms; plugin distribution and signing obligations via TAK.gov; government-purpose rights in plugins funded by SBIR/OT.
Employment law: 8 U.S.C. 1324b compliance when restricting roles to U.S. persons or cleared citizens; job-posting language.

Immigration: Indonesian founder's status pathway (O-1, H-1B, International Entrepreneur Parole; no E-2 treaty for Indonesia - verify), German founder's PR timeline and travel constraints during adjustment.

Corporate structure: Delaware C-corp, founder IP assignment, 83(b), whether an EU/German subsidiary is warranted for NATO DIANA/German channels and how control and ITAR defense-service rules interact.
Allied-market export compliance: German AWG/BAFA and EU dual-use rules if development occurs in Germany; ITAR/EAR re-export rules for any U.S.-origin controlled content.
Hardware-adjacent rules if any edge device is sold: Section 889, NDAA component prohibitions, TAA/Buy American where applicable.
Fraud and false-certification exposure in SBIR/SAM.gov representations (GAO-24-105470) and the need for documented eligibility files.

can_start_unclassified_or_commercial: ATAK-CIV plugins and TAK Server tooling for public safety, disaster response, border/critical infrastructure and allied civil users, with a later military plugin track via TAK.gov (S06, S01).
Public-safety/emergency-management common operating picture built on open standards (CoT, OGC, MIL-STD-2525) sold to state/local/federal civil agencies, positioned for DoD experimentation (S01).
Data-integration middleware and translators for unclassified/coalition-releasable data using public NATO FMN/STANAG profiles (S03, S12).
Commercial-imagery and OSINT PED analytics on commercial EO/SAR and public datasets, sold to civil and commercial buyers and to DoD via CDAO/NGA commercial channels (S05).
DDIL-tolerant data synchronization and store-and-forward software over commercial radios/SATCOM, cryptography via standard libraries (S02, S03).
